title: Decimal place value: reading and comparing decimals

pedagogy.rationale: Place value is modelled on a chart, then practised with support that fades to independent work, with misconceptions about decimal length addressed directly.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Can name the value of a digit in a whole number up to thousands (the 4 in 3,482 is worth 400).
Knows that one tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole, so 3 tenths is 3/10.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a decimal with more digits after the point is larger, so 0.125 > 0.5 because 125 > 5.
misconceptions.response: Compare place by place from the left. 0.5 has 5 tenths; 0.125 has only 1 tenth, so 0.5 is larger.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a decimal with fewer digits is larger because tenths are bigger than hundredths, so 0.4 > 0.45.
misconceptions.response: Write both to the same number of places: 0.40 and 0.45. Same tenths, so compare hundredths: 5 > 0, so 0.45 is larger.

misconceptions.description: Names the places after the point like whole-number places (tens, hundreds) or counts a 'oneths' place.
misconceptions.response: There is no oneths place. The first place after the point is tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.

misconceptions.description: Ignores a zero after the point, reading 0.05 as five tenths.
misconceptions.response: The zero holds the tenths place empty, so the 5 sits in the hundredths place: 0.05 is five hundredths.

scenes.title: Which bag of rice is heavier?
scenes.learnerAction: Read the two scale readings and guess which bag is heavier.

content.body:
At the market, Musu weighs two small bags of rice. One scale shows **1.5 kg**. The other shows **1.25 kg**.

Her brother says the second bag is heavier because 25 is bigger than 5. Is he right? By the end of this lesson you will know, and you will be able to explain why.

scenes.title: What you will learn
scenes.learnerAction: Read the two goals for today.

content.body:
Today you will learn to:

1. Name the place and value of any digit in a decimal, up to thousandths.
2. Compare and order decimals by checking place by place, and explain which is larger.

At the end you will show both on your own, without help.

scenes.title: Warm-up: what do you already know?

content.body: Two quick questions about ideas we will build on. If either one is hard, tell your teacher: you will get a short review first.

options.feedback: The 4 is not in the ones place. Count from the right: ones, tens, hundreds.
Yes. The 4 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 4 hundreds, 400.
40 would put the 4 in the tens place. It is one place further left.

items.prompt: Which means the same as 3 tenths?

options.feedback: Yes. A tenth is one of ten equal parts, so 3 tenths is 3/10.
3/100 is 3 hundredths, parts of a whole cut into 100 pieces.
30 is a whole number. Tenths are parts of one whole.

scenes.title: The decimal place-value chart
scenes.learnerAction: Study the chart and say the value of each digit in 3.472.

content.body:
The decimal point separates whole ones from parts of a one. Places after the point are **tenths**, **hundredths** and **thousandths**. Each place is worth one tenth of the place to its left.

In **3.472**: the 3 is 3 ones (3), the 4 is 4 tenths (0.4), the 7 is 7 hundredths (0.07) and the 2 is 2 thousandths (0.002).
keyPoints: There is no 'oneths' place: the first place after the point is tenths.
Read 3.472 as three and four hundred seventy-two thousandths.

scenes.title: Worked example: every digit of 15.258
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step and check the value of each digit.

content.body: The number 15.258 has two 5s. They are worth very different amounts because they sit in different places. Reveal one step at a time.

steps.label: Find the point
steps.description: Everything left of the point is whole ones and tens: 15. Everything right of it is parts: .258.

steps.label: Whole part
steps.description: The 1 is 1 ten (10). The first 5 is 5 ones (5).

steps.label: First place after the point
steps.description: The 2 is in the tenths place: 2 tenths, 0.2.

steps.label: Second place
steps.description: The second 5 is in the hundredths place: 5 hundredths, 0.05.

steps.label: Third place
steps.description: The 8 is in the thousandths place: 8 thousandths, 0.008.

accessibility.textAlternative: Six revealed steps naming the value of each digit of 15.258: 10, 5, 0.2, 0.05 and 0.008.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Enter to reveal each step, then Continue.

offline.note: Steps are saved with the lesson.

scenes.title: Zeros hold a place
scenes.learnerAction: Answer two questions about zeros, using the chart.

content.body: A zero after the point keeps a place empty, so the digits after it move one place to the right. Use the chart for these two.

options.feedback: The 0 fills the tenths place, so the 7 is pushed into the hundredths place.
Yes. The 0 holds the tenths place, so the 7 is in the hundredths place.
The 7 is to the right of the point, so it is part of a one.
0.5 is five tenths. Hundredths need a second place after the point.
0.005 is five thousandths: the 5 is three places after the point.
Yes. Zero tenths, then 5 in the hundredths place.

hints: Write the number in the chart, one digit per column.

scenes.title: Worked example: 1.5 or 1.25?
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step to settle Musu's question.

content.body: To compare decimals, line up the points and compare place by place from the left. The first place that differs decides.

steps.label: Line up the points
steps.description: Write 1.5 above 1.25 so the points are in one column.

steps.label: Fill empty places
steps.description: Write 1.5 as 1.50. Adding a zero at the end does not change the value.

steps.label: Compare ones
steps.description: Both have 1 one. Same, so move right.

steps.label: Decide
steps.description: 1.5 > 1.25. The 1.5 kg bag is heavier. Having more digits did not make 1.25 larger.

accessibility.textAlternative: Five revealed steps comparing 1.50 and 1.25 by lining up the points and comparing ones, then tenths.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Enter to reveal each step, then Continue.

scenes.title: Try comparing with a hint
scenes.learnerAction: Compare each pair. Use the hint if you need it.

content.body: Line up the points and give both numbers the same number of places before you compare.

options.feedback: Write 0.4 as 0.40. Same tenths; then 5 hundredths beats 0 hundredths.
Yes. 0.40 and 0.45 have the same tenths, and 5 hundredths > 0 hundredths.
They share 4 tenths, but 0.45 also has 5 hundredths.
125 > 5 for whole numbers, but compare tenths here: 1 tenth against 5 tenths.
Yes. 0.5 has 5 tenths; 0.125 has only 1 tenth.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two guided multiple-choice comparisons: 0.4 with 0.45, and 0.125 with 0.5.

content.body: Kollie says 2.35 is larger than 2.4 because 35 is more than 4. Sia says 2.4 is larger because it has more tenths. Who is right?

options.feedback: 35 and 4 are not whole numbers here. Compare tenths: 2.35 has 3 tenths, 2.4 has 4 tenths.
Yes. Both have 2 ones; 4 tenths > 3 tenths, so 2.4 > 2.35.

scenes.title: Your turn
scenes.learnerAction: Answer four questions on your own, then read the feedback.

content.body: Work on your own, without the chart if you can. Each answer tells you why it is right or what to check.

options.feedback: The 8 is the second digit after the point, so it is in the hundredths place.
Yes. The 8 is in the hundredths place: 8 hundredths.
The 8 is after the point, so it is part of a one.
Yes. Two zeros hold the tenths and hundredths, so the 9 is 9 thousandths.
The zeros hold places. Count three places after the point.
Count again: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

items.prompt: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?

options.feedback: This list puts the largest first. Compare tenths: 0.072 has 0 tenths.
Yes. Tenths are 0, 6 and 7, so the order is 0.072, 0.65, 0.7.
0.072 has the fewest tenths, so it is the smallest.
Write 5.1 as 5.10. Compare tenths: 0 against 1.
Yes. Both have 5 ones; 1 tenth > 0 tenths.

scenes.title: Look back and look ahead
scenes.learnerAction: Think about Musu's question again, then note what comes next.

content.body:
Go back to Musu's rice: which bag was heavier, and how do you know? Say your reason to a partner.

In one week your teacher will ask a few questions like today's again, without notes. That helps the idea stay with you. Next lesson, you will use place value to round decimals.
